note: What each grammatical term is, said plainly and with an example, for a reader who has never met it. Written by hand; data/grammar.json keeps Wiktionary's glossary, which this is read before. An example marks the word in the form with *stars*.

mood.plain: How the speaker means what the verb says: as a fact, as something wished, doubted or imagined, or as an order.

tense.plain: When it happens: before now, now, or later.

aspect.plain: How the action is seen: as one finished whole, or as going on, repeated or unfinished.

person.plain: Who does it: the speaker (I, we), the one spoken to (you), or someone else (he, she, they).

number.plain: How many: one, or more than one.

case.plain: The form a noun takes to show its job in the sentence: who does something, to whom, whose, where.

gender.plain: A class every noun belongs to, which the words around it change to match. It has little to do with sex: German das Mädchen, the girl, is neuter.

definiteness.plain: Whether something is a particular, known one (the house) or any one (a house).

declension.plain: The set of endings a noun or adjective takes, which depends on the words around it.

degree.plain: How strongly an adjective holds: big, bigger, the biggest.

voice.plain: Whether the subject does the action (she wrote it) or has it done to it (it was written).

register.plain: How formal the word is: for strangers and official writing, or for friends.

nonfinite.plain: A verb form that names the action without saying who does it or when: to go, going, gone.

dual.plain: Exactly two, in languages that have a form just for pairs.

third-person.plain: Anyone else: he, she, it, they.

nominative.plain: The one doing the action: the subject.

accusative.plain: The one the action is done to: the direct object.

dative.plain: The one something is given or done for: to whom.

genitive.plain: Whose it is, or what it is part of: of, 's.
genitive.example: *the man's* book, the roof *of the house*

vocative.plain: The form used to call or speak to someone directly.

instrumental.plain: What something is done with or by.
instrumental.example: Russian писать *ручкой*, to write *with a pen*

prepositional.plain: The form a noun takes after certain prepositions, mostly about where or about what.

ablative.plain: Away from, out of, or by means of something.

partitive.plain: Some of something, or an action not done to the end.

essive.plain: Being something for a while, as a role or state.

masculine.plain: One of the classes nouns fall into; the words around a masculine noun take its endings. Mostly a matter of the word, not of sex.

feminine.plain: One of the classes nouns fall into; the words around a feminine noun take its endings. Mostly a matter of the word, not of sex.

neuter.plain: The class of nouns that are neither masculine nor feminine.

animate.plain: Said of a noun for a person or an animal, which some languages give endings of their own.
animate.example: Russian вижу *брата*, I see my brother

inanimate.plain: Said of a noun for a thing, not a person or an animal.
inanimate.example: Russian вижу *стол*, I see the table

definite.plain: A particular one both speakers know about: the.

indefinite.plain: Any one, not yet known: a.

present.plain: Now, or always, or as a habit.

non-past.plain: Now or later: one form for both.
non-past.example: Japanese *食べる*, eat or will eat

preterite.plain: Something that happened and was over at a point in the past.

imperfect.plain: The past seen from inside: something that went on, kept happening, or used to be.
imperfect.example: Spanish *comía*, I *was eating*, I *used to eat*

perfect.plain: Done before now and still mattering now.

pluperfect.plain: Done before another moment in the past.

aorist.plain: A past action told as one complete event, the way a story tells it.

indicative.plain: The ordinary form for saying what is so: facts, and questions about them.

subjunctive.plain: The form for what is wished, wanted, doubted, feared or only imagined, rather than said to be so. It mostly comes after words like that, if, so that.
subjunctive.example: I wish he *were* here. It is vital that she *be* on time. Spanish quiero que *vengas*, I want you to come.

subjunctive-i.plain: German's form for repeating what someone else said, without vouching for it.
subjunctive-i.example: Er sagt, er *sei* krank. He says he is ill.

subjunctive-ii.plain: German's form for what is not real: wishes, polite requests, and if-only.
subjunctive-ii.example: Wenn ich Zeit *hätte*... If I had time...

conditional.plain: What would happen, if something else were so.

conditional-i.plain: What would happen, if something else were so.
conditional-i.example: German ich *würde gehen*, I would go

conditional-ii.plain: What would have happened, if something else had been so.
conditional-ii.example: German ich *wäre gegangen*, I would have gone

future-i.example: German ich *werde gehen*, I will go

future-ii.plain: Done by some point later on.
future-ii.example: German ich *werde gegangen sein*, I will have gone

imperative.plain: The form for telling someone to do something.

jussive.plain: A form for letting or telling someone, often not the listener, do something.

optative.plain: A form for wishing: may it be so.

potential.plain: A form for what is probably or possibly so.

passive.plain: The subject has the action done to it.

infinitive.plain: The verb itself, with nobody doing it yet: the form a dictionary lists it by.

participle.plain: A form of the verb that works like an adjective, and with a helper makes other tenses.

gerund.plain: A form of the verb for an action going on, or used like a noun.

imperfective.plain: The action as going on, repeated, or unfinished.

perfective.plain: The action as one finished whole.
perfective.example: Russian я *прочитал*, I read it (to the end)

positive.plain: The adjective as it is, without comparing.

strong.plain: The adjective endings German uses when no article in front shows the case.

weak.plain: The adjective endings German uses after der, die, das, where the article already shows the case.

mixed.plain: The adjective endings German uses after ein, kein, mein.

formal.plain: For strangers, elders and official writing.

polite.plain: The respectful way of saying it.
polite.example: Japanese *食べます*, (I) eat, said politely
